newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Blue Circle cements long-term pay deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Blue Circle cements long-term pay deal.

text.p: Britain's biggest cement producer, Blue Circle Industries Plc, announced a long-term pay deal with its workforce on Monday, which was immediately hailed by union leaders as a model agreement for industry under the new Labour government.
Blue Circle Cement (BCC) said that its 2,000 workers have accepted an annual pay increase for the next three years of the official Retail Price Index (RPI) measure of inflation plus 0.25 percent.

The deal, outlined in January, has been agreed between Blue Circle Cement and the GMB, Transport and General (T&G), Amalgamated Engineering and Electrical Union (AEEU) and the British Cement Staff Association trade unions.

The company said the deal promises to yield 10 million pounds in annual cost savings through "improved business efficiency and productivity, in return for guaranteed pay rises and employment security".

Unions have agreed to work with the company in trying to make the business more efficient and in return BCC has given a pledge that there will be no compulsory redundancies for at least the next three years.
The two sides have also agreed to try and extend, or roll over, the terms of the deal after the first year.
BCC, where process workers typically earn about 21,000 pounds a year, is still looking to cut the workforce by 18 percent over the next five years.
But personnel director Ross Dunn told a news conference that it was expected that at least 500 employees were likely to be attracted by redundancy packages aimed at older staff.
BCC's chief executive Ian McKenzie denied that the deal had been negotiated in anticipation of the union-backed Labour Party's election victory on May 1 after 18 years in opposition.

"We are very pleased to have reached this agreement which will improve further the competitive position of BCC and help secure the future of our UK cement operations and of employment in the long-term," he said.

But the leaders of two of Britain's biggest unions said the deal struck a chord with the Labour government's hopes of linking pay increases with job security, and hoped similar deals with other companies would follow.

"I am delighted that we have signed an agreement that breaks new ground in meeting the requirements of working people," said John Edmonds, General Secretary of the GMB union. "This is a blueprint for social partnership in Britain under a Labour government," he told a news conference.
"Everybody wins in this agreement," said Bill Morris, General Secretary of the T&G union.
"What's good for Blue Circle and its employees can also be good for other companies and for British industry."
However, the deal comes after many years of savage job cuts in the cement industry, caused by overcapacity and increased competition.
According to McKenzie BCC's own workforce has shrunk from over 9,000 people since Labour was last in power in 1979.

"Yes, you could suggest that we (the unions) should have done this (sort of deal) sooner, but is that any reason for not doing it now?," Len McCluskey, the T&G's National Secretary, told Reuters after the news conference.
